1:
Adam Clarke sets the scene as a schoolroom: the preceptor calls his pupils and tells them how he himself was educated, and Clarke maps the chapter into the teaching the father gave, the teachings received, and the exhortation to persevere in well-doing and avoid evil. The lessons, he says, were those of a wise and affectionate parent to his only son, a peculiar object of his regards and of a fond mother’s; introducing the matter this way secured attention. His own maxim closes the note: teaching by precept is good, teaching by example is better, but teaching both by precept and example is best of all.

Who the father is divides them. John Gill reports Gersom interpreting it of God as their father but prefers Solomon, and takes the children not as those of his body but as disciples who applied to him for knowledge. Charles Ellicott and John Wesley gloss it flatly as of me, your teacher; Wesley adds, of me who have paternal authority over you and affection for you. Keil and Delitzsch make the grammar carry the point: the plural address replaces the singular used hitherto because in what follows the poet is himself the son whom a father instructs, and he deliberately avoids the phrase your father, since he means not the father of each hearer but himself, a father in relation to them as his disciples, showing fatherly love and so claiming paternal authority. They add that the infinitive gives not the object of attention but its design and aim.

Matthew Henry lets the address be both, telling the teacher’s own children to attend first to instructions set down for the use of others also, and observing that magistrates and ministers entrusted with larger societies must take more than ordinary care of their own families: this charity must begin at home, though it must not end there. He notes the address is not my children but you children, remarks that only one son of Solomon’s own is on record and that he was nevertheless willing to set up for a schoolmaster and teach other people’s children, since the branch is easily bent while young and tender, and asks that grown persons come with the disposition of children, prejudices laid aside and the mind as white paper. To save the credit of parents whose children disappoint them he observes that Rehoboam was far from being either one of the wisest or one of the best, and that thousands have got more good by these proverbs than the son to whom they seem to have been dedicated.

On the sonship, Gill again reports Jarchi referring it to God and again prefers David, noting that Solomon was not an only son but a darling, beloved of the Lord and so named Jedidiah, and beloved of his father. Henry adds that the covenant was entailed on him as on Isaac, and guesses David was the stricter with him for having seen the effects of indulgence in Adonijah, whom he had never crossed in anything, and in Absalom. Ellicott finds the notices of these early years in good agreement with the historical books, identifies tender as the epithet his father applied to him, and traces the other word from an original sense of only, through beloved as an only son — so of Isaac while Ishmael was living, and here of Solomon though Bath-sheba had other children by David — to the Greek renderings only-begotten and well-beloved, applied in their highest sense to Christ. Wesley reads tender as young in years and tenderly educated, and holds that the following verses, at least as far as the tenth, are the words of David. Gill takes the wisdom to be got as Christ himself, possessed by faith; Ellicott likens it to the pearl of great price; Clarke says only that true religion is essential to happiness.
6:
The seventh verse is the crux, and three of them will not read it as it stands. Charles Ellicott offers the alternative outright: the beginning of wisdom is, Get wisdom, and at the price of all thou hast gotten get understanding. Keil and Delitzsch build the same rendering into an argument — wisdom begins with the striving after it, and that striving is itself its fundamental beginning — and set it against the motto of the book, where the fear of the Lord is the subject standing foremost, whereas here the beginning of wisdom is the subject and what that beginning consists in is the thing to be said. Adam Clarke renders the opening words as wisdom is the principle and calls the knowledge of the true God the leaping point of all religion, adding under the Christian dispensation the knowledge of Jesus Christ and of the salvation he bought with his own blood. Clarke then opens a small textual dossier: Coverdale renders the verse very remarkably but by paraphrase rather than translation, his own old manuscript Bible with great simplicity, the whole verse is wanting in the Arabic and in the best copies of the Septuagint, and the Complutensian Polyglot puts understanding for wisdom in the first clause, so that the verse asks twice for the same thing.

Clarke also draws the distinction the verse turns on. Wisdom prescribes the best end and the means best calculated to attain it; understanding directs to the ways, times, places and opportunities of practising it. Wisdom points out the thing requisite, understanding sees to its attainment; wisdom sees, but understanding feels; one discovers, the other possesses. He warns against being content with a sound creed, since devils believe and tremble.

On the exalting of the eighth verse the versions pull apart. John Gill reports the Talmudists making the word a diligent search that turns things about until what is sought is found, and the Greek interpreters taking it in that sense of searching. Keil and Delitzsch treat the word as occurring only here and fix it from its parallel, approving the reading that makes it a buyer holding the thing high in price and raising his offer upon offer, and rejecting the Greek that has it circumvallated, surrounded with a wall, as a strange and here unsuitable figure; they note also that the performance and its consequence are transposed across the two clauses. Ellicott simply sets beside it the promise that those who honour God are honoured, and John Wesley glosses exalting as giving her the highest esteem and affection.

Gill reads the whole passage of Christ. To forsake wisdom is to forsake the assembly, the ministers, the word and ordinances, to drop the doctrines or quit the profession; nominal professors may do so finally and totally, true believers only partially and for a time. The principal thing is the principal person, above angels and above the greatest and best of men, King to kings, High Priest to priests, Prophet, Shepherd, Master of the family, Head of the body, Foundation and Corner Stone. The ornament of grace he takes as an increase of grace, justifying grace covering the nakedness of the soul and sanctifying grace being the beauty of holiness; Wesley keeps it a literal head ornament of the kind then worn, and Clarke says a diadem is no more honourable to its princely wearer than sound wisdom to the Christian and the scholar, quoting the aphorism that knowledge is power and adding that learning is respected only where the learned man is consistent and not overbearing. Keil and Delitzsch, reaching the tenth verse, deny that the father’s admonition has now passed over into warnings of the poet’s own, as Hitzig held; the instruction so far has been general and the specific teaching still to come.
10:
Whose voice is this? Matthew Henry reports that some carry the father’s instructions to the end of the chapter and some to the end of the ninth, but thinks the teacher begins again here, if not sooner; John Gill notes the same opinion and reaches the same answer. Adam Clarke makes the promise of many years a medical one: intemperance shortens the days of the wicked, and the principal part of our diseases springs from indolence, intemperance and disorderly passions, and religion, by exciting industry and sober habits, prevents them. He reads the unstraitened steps commercially: a man who ponders his paths, serves no by-ends and uses neither trick nor cunning can never be embarrassed, and runs without stumbling when a favourable tide of Providence calls for increased exertion. Gill takes the same clause of enemies and obstructions, and of saints in a large place.

The command to avoid the path is read three ways. Gill reports the Latin turning it into a warning not to delight in those paths, and objects that delight supposes continuance whereas what is forbidden is the first step; he also reports Jarchi and Gersom taking the verb not as flee but as make void, hindering the wicked from their designs. Keil and Delitzsch give the word its fundamental sense of going aside rather than the bad sense it elsewhere carries, glossing the next word so that thou come not to stand upon it, and making the last verb coincide with escaping. Clarke and Henry both escalate: Clarke asks that no worldly gain bring one near the way one would not wish to be found in when called into the eternal world, and bids the reader run for his life; Henry says the caution is not to keep a due distance but a great one, and compares such company with a house infected with the plague entered by one who thinks himself guarded with an antidote.

At the sleepless verse Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch independently quote the same line of Virgil, the taunt that had the man not found some mischief to do he would have died. Clarke takes the verse literally of night robbery, booty being had before rest, though he grants some are so malevolent that the sight of another in prosperity puts them to excessive pain. Gill has them restless as the troubled sea that casts up mire and dirt, and asks who would keep such company. Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both call the practice of evil a second nature, Keil and Delitzsch adding that to interrupt it would be like interrupting a diet and would make them ill, and that the marginal reading rightly makes the verb causative, the opposite of helping.

The bread of wickedness divides them. Gill offers both senses; John Wesley takes wickedness itself to be as pleasant to them as bread; Ellicott takes it of bread acquired by wickedness; Keil and Delitzsch argue the first from the parallel, since had the poet meant wickedness as their food he must have used another word in the second clause, and note that the change of tense shows them washing the bread down with the wine. Clarke turns both into crimes, stealing and highway robbery.

On the shining path Clarke works out the optics: the sun is still below the horizon, his light increasing by reflection through the atmosphere until the prepared day comes at its determined time, the wise man being here below only in his twilight. Henry insists the light is growing, not a meteor nor a candle that burns down but the rising sun, perfect only in heaven; Wesley has the just growing daily till all is swallowed up in glory. Keil and Delitzsch, finding that the next verse joins the preceding one without needing a particle, judge it likelier that the two have been transposed than that a conjunction stands out of place.
20:
Four of them refuse the received rendering of the verse on the heart. Adam Clarke gives it as above all keeping, guard thy heart; Charles Ellicott as above all things that are to be guarded; Matthew Henry reports both senses, keep them with all keepings, there being many ways of keeping and all little enough; and Keil and Delitzsch weigh whether the noun names the thing avoided or the object watched, and settle on the second. John Gill keeps diligence but slips the alternative in as a comment: though kingdoms, cities, families and treasures are to be kept, the heart is to be kept above all.

On the issues of life Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch arrive at the same physiology. Clarke renders the phrase the goings out of lives and asks whether it is not a plain allusion to the arteries carrying blood from the heart to its utmost extremities, since while the heart can propel the blood life continues; the fountain must not be stopped up. Keil and Delitzsch, defining the noun as the point from which a thing goes forth and the course proceeding from it, infer that the heart fixes not only the source of life but its direction, and call it the pitcher at the blood-fountain which draws the blood and pours it forth, and into which it disembogues. Henry keeps the moral sense: all the actions of life flow from the heart, so keeping it is making the tree good and healing the springs. Ellicott lets the issues run to death as well as life, and John Wesley reads the heart as thoughts, will and affections.

The command about the feet splits them cleanly. Gill takes it as weighing the path in the balances of thought, as Aben Ezra has it, and notes that the Greek makes it straight paths instead; Henry has the word mean weigh, putting the word of God in one scale and the action in the other; Clarke and Wesley make it deliberation before acting. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch reject that sense: the verb means make the path smooth and level, taking the obstacles out of it. Keil and Delitzsch allow that the word once means to weigh out, from the name of a steelyard, but everywhere else to make even and open a road, so the admonition concerns not measuring a way but clearing it; they add that an Arabic word alleged to mean a balance, printed in the newest editions of a standard lexicon, is without evidence.

At the close both stop over a passage the Hebrew does not have. Clarke quotes the verse the Greek and the Latin add, a promise that God will make the paths straight and conduct the journeyings in peace, finds nothing like it in the Hebrew, Chaldee or Syriac though it stands in five of his manuscripts, notes that De Lyra rejects it as a gloss on no authority, and concludes that if it is an addition it is an ancient one and its promise true whether authentic or not. Keil and Delitzsch, having tried to render the added lines back into Hebrew, call them by no means genuine, since it takes right and left in another sense than the verse it follows and promises as God’s work what that verse requires of man, a poverty of style that betrays the imitator; and they defend the Hebrew verse itself, which Hitzig disputed, as continuing the preceding one.

Ellicott finds the word for froward mouth to mean distortion, a twisting of the truth; Henry says such a mouth is as ill-favoured before God as a mouth drawn awry is before men. On the fixed eyes Keil and Delitzsch commend concentration against dissipation, quoting an ancient warning against staring about the streets of a city, and connecting the rule with the demand for a single and not a squinting eye.
